evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper, an analysis of water management in Ecuador is conducted through a review of legal policies, environmental data, economic frameworks, and social studies related to water access.

This search yielded 1043 articles, of which the 25 most-relevant articles were reviewed. Next, a literature review of peer-reviewed articles in the same databases was performed to evaluate water and environmental quality parameters in Ecuador. This step yielded 6520 total articles, of which the 30 most salient were reviewed.

criterion_notes.c1: Among broader water-resource and pollution themes, the paper discusses household and community drinking-water and sanitation access in Ecuador, including community drinking-water management via Juntas de Agua Potable (Section 3.1.5), urban vs. rural public sewer connections (Section 3.2.3), and household coping strategies for unreliable water supplies (Sections 3.4.1-3.4.2).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — the paper reviews Ecuadorian constitutional, statutory, regulatory, and governance frameworks for water (2008 Constitution, Ley Organica, TULSMA, NTE INEN 1108, SENAGUA/Ministerio del Ambiente y Agua, WUAs/Juntas de Agua, PES, and pollution taxes). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes (descriptively, in part) — although most of the paper covers macro-governance background, ambient/potable physicochemical quality norms, and extractive-industry pollution, Section 3.1.5 explicitly describes local rule-type mechanisms governing community water access in Juntas de Agua (mandatory minga labor vs. monthly bill payment and suspension of water access for non-participation) and Section 3.1.2 describes state authorization rules for community-financed infrastructure. Under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow reading, however, the overall decision is exclude (E05) because the paper is a non-systematic narrative review with no primary empirical data.
criterion_notes.c3: No primary quantitative, qualitative, or socio-legal empirical data are collected or analyzed. Although Section 2 reports running four thematic searches in Environment Complete and ScienceDirect, it is a narrative policy/literature overview rather than a systematic empirical synthesis: it reports no search strings, no inclusion or exclusion criteria, no reproducible screening procedure (arbitrarily reviewing the 25 most-relevant, 30 most salient, 16 prominent, and 29 most-relevant articles across four broad topics), no study-level extraction table or quality assessment, and no structured empirical synthesis -> E05.
criterion_notes.c4: The text cites secondary national statistics on drinking-water, sanitation, and public sewer connection coverage (pp. 2, 8) and narratively mentions WUA water-access suspension (p. 6) and household coping with unreliable supplies (pp. 12-13) from prior literature, but neither measures nor systematically synthesizes an empirical service-access outcome linked to a governance exposure.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the article is a broad four-part narrative overview spanning national water legislation, industrial/agricultural/sewage pollution, economic instruments, and social protests, it lacks a defined empirical study population/unit of analysis, a specific exposure-outcome analytic pair, and an empirical or systematic-review study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Narrative literature and policy review (non-systematic review)
population_and_sample: Ecuador (narrative review of national legislation and 25, 30, 16, and 29 selected peer-reviewed articles across four thematic searches; no primary empirical sample)
exposure: Ecuadorian water governance, legal authorization, environmental quality regulations, economic instruments, and community WUA rules (2008 Constitution, Ley Organica, TULSMA, NTE INEN 1108, Juntas de Agua minga/fee rules, PES, pollution taxes)
outcome: Narrative overview of environmental water quality, resource allocation, secondary sanitation/sewer coverage figures, household coping practices, and water protests (no primary or systematically synthesized empirical access outcome)
rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the paper discusses water and sanitation governance and access in Ecuador—including constitutional/statutory water law and community WUA minga/fee and suspension rules—it collects no primary empirical data and is not a systematic empirical synthesis. Section 2 describes a broad thematic narrative review of Ecuadorian statutes and arbitrarily selected subsets of secondary articles (25, 30, 16, and 29 articles from four database searches without reported search terms, eligibility criteria, reproducible screening, study tables, or structured synthesis). Decision is exclude under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording.
